cheat_sheet.title: Complexity, Searching and Sorting — Structural Cheat Sheet
cheat_sheet.introduction: This sheet turns Complexity, Searching and Sorting into visible relationships. It is a reference for planning, tracing, debugging, and explaining—not a list to memorize.
cheat_sheet.why_it_matters: The level contributes directly to a interview-ready algorithm solution set. Each concept helps the learner move from an ambiguous task to a contract, a representation, a verified transition, and an explainable result.

mental_model.summary: Represent the work as input-output contracts, invariants, trace tables, and complexity comparisons before translating it into implementation details.
reasoning_cycle: Model variables, state, constraints, and relationships

input_questions: What may be absent or malformed?
output_questions: What shape and state are promised?

core_concepts.title: Stable comparison sorting

common_mistakes: Starting with syntax before defining the input-output contract.
Combining current state and a candidate update so rejection cannot be safe.
Treating an observed normal result as proof for every boundary.
Choosing a structure because it is familiar rather than because its operations match the constraints.
Ignoring empty, missing, duplicate, maximum-size, repeated, or out-of-order cases.
Hiding failures instead of representing loading, empty, rejected, and error states explicitly.
Optimizing before measuring the actual bottleneck or risk.
Explaining what the implementation does without explaining why its invariant proves correctness.

Did the repair pass the original failure and nearby regression cases?

lessons.title: Input size and operation counting
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Input size and operation counting within a timed but explainable problem-solving scenario.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Input size and operation counting to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Input size and operation counting is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Define input size, identify the repeated primitive operation, and express how its count grows as input scales.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Input size and operation counting, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use input-output contracts, invariants, trace tables, and complexity comparisons. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

inputs: The data or event that activates Input size and operation counting
outputs: A value, decision, or visible state matching the contract
A preserved or deliberately updated next state
Evidence explaining acceptance or rejection

variables_and_state.name: candidate_input
variables_and_state.role: The untrusted or unverified incoming value

variables_and_state.name: current_state
variables_and_state.role: The last state known to satisfy all invariants

variables_and_state.name: constraint_result
variables_and_state.role: The explicit validation outcome

variables_and_state.name: next_state
variables_and_state.role: A proposed state computed without corrupting current_state

constraints: Inputs must match the declared shape and permitted boundary.
A rejected input must not corrupt the previous valid state.
The output must be representable by the current application workflow.
Every external or user-provided value is validated before use.
invariants: The governing relationship remains true: Define input size, identify the repeated primitive operation, and express how its count grows as input scales.
At most one documented commit occurs for one accepted transition.
Invalid input leaves the last valid state unchanged.
step_by_step_reasoning: Restate the problem as a testable input-output contract.
List state variables and separate current state from a candidate update.
Write constraints as predicates with visible boundary choices.
Apply the structural rule for Input size and operation counting.
Trace the normal case one transition at a time.
Trace an exact boundary and one invalid case.
Compare observed output and preserved invariants with the contract.
Record the first divergent state if the check fails.

worked_examples.scenario: A learner applies Input size and operation counting while building a timed but explainable problem-solving scenario.

Trace the transition and compare the result with the contract.

worked_examples.scenario: The input is exactly at the smallest or largest documented valid boundary.
worked_examples.input: A boundary value explicitly included by the constraint.
reasoning: Write the inclusive or exclusive boundary symbolically.
Evaluate the predicate before changing state.
Apply the same rule used for ordinary valid input.
Verify that the output remains representable and accessible.
worked_examples.output: The boundary case is accepted once and produces a valid output without special hidden state.

worked_examples.title: Rejected case: preserve the invariant
worked_examples.scenario: An input violates one required relationship or arrives in an unsupported state.
worked_examples.input: An out-of-contract value paired with a previously valid state.
reasoning: Identify the failed constraint and stop before commit.
Keep the previous valid state unchanged.
Return a specific, non-sensitive explanation or recovery path.
Record the case as evidence for a regression check.
worked_examples.output: A controlled rejection, preserved prior state, and actionable feedback.

common_mistakes: Beginning implementation before defining the required output.
Changing state before the input or transition has been validated.
Memorizing the label 'Input size and operation counting' without applying its governing relationship.
Testing only one convenient normal case and assuming boundaries behave identically.
edge_cases: The smallest valid input or empty valid structure, when allowed.
The largest documented input, count, depth, size, or duration.
A duplicate, repeated event, retry, or already-completed transition.
Malformed, missing, stale, unauthorized, or otherwise out-of-contract input.
debugging_strategy: Freeze the first input that produces a wrong observable result.
Write the expected trace beside the observed trace.
Locate the first row where state, constraint, or output diverges.
Repair the rule or boundary responsible for that first divergence.
Rerun the failing case plus one normal, one boundary, and one rejection case.
progressive_hints: Label the input and promised output before naming any tool or syntax.
Separate current_state from next_state and write the validity predicate.
Apply this rule, then trace the boundary: Define input size, identify the repeated primitive operation, and express how its count grows as input scales.
lessons.summary: Input size and operation counting is mastered when the learner can model its inputs and state, apply the rule 'Define input size, identify the repeated primitive operation, and express how its count grows as input scales.', and prove the result with normal, boundary, and rejected traces.

checkpoint_questions.prompt: What must be written before implementation begins?
checkpoint_questions.answer: The input-output contract and constraints.

Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Stable comparison sorting is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. A stable sort preserves the input order of equal keys, which matters when records have earlier ordering decisions.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Stable comparison sorting, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Selecting and explaining an algorithm is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Choose from input properties, operation costs, memory, stability, worst-case guarantees, and implementation risk, then justify the trade-off.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Selecting and explaining an algorithm, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

project.title: Complexity, Searching and Sorting: Interview-Ready Algorithm Solution Set
project.real_world_context: A small team needs a timed but explainable problem-solving scenario that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate interview-ready algorithm solution set that demonstrates all eight skills from Complexity, Searching and Sorting. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: Define input size, identify the repeated primitive operation, and express how its count grows as input scales.
Asymptotic bounds compare growth while ignoring constant factors, but auxiliary memory and real constraints still affect choice.
Linear search preserves that the target is absent from the processed prefix and stops on discovery or exhaustion.
Binary search maintains a sorted candidate interval containing every possible answer and removes a proven half each step.
A stable sort preserves the input order of equal keys, which matters when records have earlier ordering decisions.
Merge sort divides, solves smaller arrays, and merges sorted sequences; quicksort partitions around a pivot with data-dependent balance.
Counting or bucket methods exploit bounded key structure to avoid comparison lower bounds at a memory cost.
Choose from input properties, operation costs, memory, stability, worst-case guarantees, and implementation risk, then justify the trade-off.

first divergence, repair, trade-off, and next iteration

The diagram disagrees with the implemented flow.

Submission evidence cannot be reproduced.

lessons.title: Monotonic stacks and next-boundary problems
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Monotonic stacks and next-boundary problems within a timed but explainable problem-solving scenario.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Monotonic stacks and next-boundary problems to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Monotonic stacks and next-boundary problems is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. A monotonic stack keeps unresolved candidates in order and removes those resolved by the current value.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Monotonic stacks and next-boundary problems, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use input-output contracts, invariants, trace tables, and complexity comparisons. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

inputs: The data or event that activates Monotonic stacks and next-boundary problems
outputs: A value, decision, or visible state matching the contract
A preserved or deliberately updated next state
Evidence explaining acceptance or rejection

variables_and_state.name: candidate_input
variables_and_state.role: The untrusted or unverified incoming value

variables_and_state.name: current_state
variables_and_state.role: The last state known to satisfy all invariants

variables_and_state.name: constraint_result
variables_and_state.role: The explicit validation outcome

variables_and_state.name: next_state
variables_and_state.role: A proposed state computed without corrupting current_state

constraints: Inputs must match the declared shape and permitted boundary.
A rejected input must not corrupt the previous valid state.
The output must be representable by the current application workflow.
Every external or user-provided value is validated before use.
invariants: The governing relationship remains true: A monotonic stack keeps unresolved candidates in order and removes those resolved by the current value.
At most one documented commit occurs for one accepted transition.
Invalid input leaves the last valid state unchanged.
step_by_step_reasoning: Restate the problem as a testable input-output contract.

Write constraints as predicates with visible boundary choices.

Trace the normal case one transition at a time.
Trace an exact boundary and one invalid case.
Compare observed output and preserved invariants with the contract.
Record the first divergent state if the check fails.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Pattern selection and counterexamples is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Pointer and window methods require order or monotonicity; construct counterexamples before applying them to arbitrary constraints.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Pattern selection and counterexamples, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

project.title: Two Pointers, Sliding Windows and Prefix Structures: Interview-Ready Algorithm Solution Set
project.real_world_context: A small team needs a timed but explainable problem-solving scenario that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate interview-ready algorithm solution set that demonstrates all eight skills from Two Pointers, Sliding Windows and Prefix Structures. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Recursive contracts and base cases within a timed but explainable problem-solving scenario.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Recursive contracts and base cases is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. A recursive function solves one state by reducing it to smaller states and needs base cases that cover every terminating path.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Recursive contracts and base cases, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use input-output contracts, invariants, trace tables, and complexity comparisons. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Call stacks and recurrence traces is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Each call owns parameters and local state; the call tree reveals repeated work and maximum stack depth.

Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

lessons.title: Backtracking state and undo

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Backtracking state and undo is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Choose, explore, and undo so every branch starts from the same valid prefix state.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Backtracking state and undo, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.body: Pruning invalid and dominated branches is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Pruning is correct only when a predicate proves that no completion of the current partial state can improve or satisfy the answer.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Pruning invalid and dominated branches, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use input-output contracts, invariants, trace tables, and complexity comparisons. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

inputs: The data or event that activates Pruning invalid and dominated branches
outputs: A value, decision, or visible state matching the contract
A preserved or deliberately updated next state
Evidence explaining acceptance or rejection

variables_and_state.role: The untrusted or unverified incoming value

variables_and_state.name: current_state
variables_and_state.role: The last state known to satisfy all invariants

variables_and_state.name: constraint_result
variables_and_state.role: The explicit validation outcome

variables_and_state.name: next_state
variables_and_state.role: A proposed state computed without corrupting current_state

constraints: Inputs must match the declared shape and permitted boundary.
A rejected input must not corrupt the previous valid state.
The output must be representable by the current application workflow.
Every external or user-provided value is validated before use.
invariants: The governing relationship remains true: Pruning is correct only when a predicate proves that no completion of the current partial state can improve or satisfy the answer.
At most one documented commit occurs for one accepted transition.
Invalid input leaves the last valid state unchanged.
step_by_step_reasoning: Restate the problem as a testable input-output contract.
List state variables and separate current state from a candidate update.
Write constraints as predicates with visible boundary choices.
Apply the structural rule for Pruning invalid and dominated branches.
Trace the normal case one transition at a time.
Trace an exact boundary and one invalid case.
Compare observed output and preserved invariants with the contract.
Record the first divergent state if the check fails.

Evaluate the predicate before changing state.

worked_examples.title: Rejected case: preserve the invariant

reasoning: Identify the failed constraint and stop before commit.
Keep the previous valid state unchanged.
Return a specific, non-sensitive explanation or recovery path.
Record the case as evidence for a regression check.
worked_examples.output: A controlled rejection, preserved prior state, and actionable feedback.

common_mistakes: Beginning implementation before defining the required output.
Changing state before the input or transition has been validated.
Memorizing the label 'Pruning invalid and dominated branches' without applying its governing relationship.
Testing only one convenient normal case and assuming boundaries behave identically.
edge_cases: The smallest valid input or empty valid structure, when allowed.
The largest documented input, count, depth, size, or duration.
A duplicate, repeated event, retry, or already-completed transition.
Malformed, missing, stale, unauthorized, or otherwise out-of-contract input.
debugging_strategy: Freeze the first input that produces a wrong observable result.
Write the expected trace beside the observed trace.
Locate the first row where state, constraint, or output diverges.
Repair the rule or boundary responsible for that first divergence.
Rerun the failing case plus one normal, one boundary, and one rejection case.

project.title: Recursion, Backtracking and Greedy Reasoning: Interview-Ready Algorithm Solution Set
project.real_world_context: A small team needs a timed but explainable problem-solving scenario that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate interview-ready algorithm solution set that demonstrates all eight skills from Recursion, Backtracking and Greedy Reasoning. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

Choose, explore, and undo so every branch starts from the same valid prefix state.
Pruning is correct only when a predicate proves that no completion of the current partial state can improve or satisfy the answer.
State representation and start boundaries determine whether order matters and whether equal choices create duplicate solutions.
A greedy method is valid when a locally preferred choice can be exchanged into some optimal solution without reducing quality.

lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Memoization and tabulation within a timed but explainable problem-solving scenario.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Memoization and tabulation to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Memoization and tabulation is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Memoization explores needed states top-down; tabulation orders all relevant states bottom-up according to dependencies.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Memoization and tabulation, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use input-output contracts, invariants, trace tables, and complexity comparisons. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

inputs: The data or event that activates Memoization and tabulation
outputs: A value, decision, or visible state matching the contract
A preserved or deliberately updated next state
Evidence explaining acceptance or rejection

Invalid input leaves the last valid state unchanged.

lessons.title: Knapsack-style choice DP
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Knapsack-style choice DP within a timed but explainable problem-solving scenario.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Knapsack-style choice DP to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Knapsack-style choice DP is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Choice states track an item boundary and limited resource; iteration direction determines whether an item may be reused.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Knapsack-style choice DP, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use input-output contracts, invariants, trace tables, and complexity comparisons. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

inputs: The data or event that activates Knapsack-style choice DP
outputs: A value, decision, or visible state matching the contract
A preserved or deliberately updated next state
Evidence explaining acceptance or rejection

variables_and_state.role: The untrusted or unverified incoming value

variables_and_state.role: The last state known to satisfy all invariants

variables_and_state.role: The explicit validation outcome

variables_and_state.name: next_state
variables_and_state.role: A proposed state computed without corrupting current_state

A rejected input must not corrupt the previous valid state.
The output must be representable by the current application workflow.
Every external or user-provided value is validated before use.
invariants: The governing relationship remains true: Choice states track an item boundary and limited resource; iteration direction determines whether an item may be reused.
At most one documented commit occurs for one accepted transition.
Invalid input leaves the last valid state unchanged.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Space optimization and correctness proof is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Discard old DP layers only after proving no future transition depends on them, and state the invariant for the compressed array.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Space optimization and correctness proof, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

project.title: Dynamic Programming and Optimization: Interview-Ready Algorithm Solution Set
project.real_world_context: A small team needs a timed but explainable problem-solving scenario that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate interview-ready algorithm solution set that demonstrates all eight skills from Dynamic Programming and Optimization. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: Dynamic programming applies when optimal solutions combine optimal subproblem results and the same states recur.
A DP state must contain exactly the information needed to evaluate future choices without remembering the entire history.
A transition combines already solved predecessor states, forming an acyclic dependency graph or a controlled iterative process.
Memoization explores needed states top-down; tabulation orders all relevant states bottom-up according to dependencies.
Sequence states often represent the best answer for a prefix or endpoint, with transitions considering the final decision.
Grid states aggregate valid predecessor paths or costs while boundaries encode unreachable or base positions.
Choice states track an item boundary and limited resource; iteration direction determines whether an item may be reused.
Discard old DP layers only after proving no future transition depends on them, and state the invariant for the compressed array.

constraints: Use only the languages, components, or structural interactions supported by the target application environment.
Do not hide invalid input, unavailable data, or failure behind a successful-looking state.
Keep current valid state recoverable until a candidate transition passes validation.
Do not embed secrets, real credentials, personal data, or private endpoints.
Make all important output and error states accessible and testable.
Record assumptions and unsupported cases explicitly.
The submitted result must be reproducible from the included instructions.

test_cases.condition: second valid input with different data

test_cases.expected: accepted only if contract includes it

test_cases.condition: valid retry after a controlled failure

debugging_checklist: Freeze a reproducible failing input.
Compare expected and observed traces.
Find the first divergent state.
Check the constraint at that transition.
Repair cause before symptoms.
Rerun the failure and adjacent cases.
Confirm state recovery and accessible feedback.
Record the limitation if the case remains unsupported.
completion_checklist: All eight level skills appear in the artifact or evidence.
The input-output contract is complete.
The structural model matches the implementation or decision flow.
All eight required test categories have evidence.
The rubric self-score totals 100 possible points.
No secret, real credential, or sensitive personal data is included.
Submission instructions reproduce the result.
Reflection names one failure, repair, and justified improvement.
submission_requirements: README with setup or review instructions

rubric.evidence: inputs, outputs, constraints, diagram, and milestones
mandatory behavior matches the project contract
clear responsibilities, transitions, and dependency boundaries
normal, boundary, invalid, repeated, and failure cases
usable states, safe handling, and recovery feedback
setup, decisions, limitations, evidence, and reproducible instructions
first divergence, repair, trade-off, and next iteration

common_failure_conditions: The result handles only one normal case.
State changes before validation.
A level skill is named but not demonstrated.
The diagram disagrees with the implemented flow.
A failed dependency leaves a false success state.
Submission evidence cannot be reproduced.
reflection_questions: Which assumption changed after the first trace?
Where did expected and observed state first diverge?
Which invariant prevented the most serious failure?
What trade-off did you make among clarity, cost, performance, accessibility, safety, or flexibility?
What evidence would you collect before a wider release?
optional_extensions: Add a second representation and compare which relationships become easier to inspect.
Add property-based or generated boundary cases without duplicating existing tests.
Measure one performance, quality, or risk indicator and justify an improvement threshold.
Design a migration or compatibility plan for one changed requirement.
project.acceptable_outcome_example: A submission may use the supplied contract and state templates, implement one complete primary journey, show all required failure states, and provide eight passing test records plus one documented limitation. The exact implementation remains the learner's work.

prompts.prompt: Restate the final input-output contract in one sentence.
Describe the first state where expected and observed behavior diverged.
Explain the repair and the invariant or constraint it restored.
Name one design trade-off and the evidence behind your choice.
What is the safest and most valuable next improvement?

common_mistakes: Starting with syntax before defining the input-output contract.
Combining current state and a candidate update so rejection cannot be safe.
Treating an observed normal result as proof for every boundary.
Choosing a structure because it is familiar rather than because its operations match the constraints.
Ignoring empty, missing, duplicate, maximum-size, repeated, or out-of-order cases.
Hiding failures instead of representing loading, empty, rejected, and error states explicitly.
Optimizing before measuring the actual bottleneck or risk.
Explaining what the implementation does without explaining why its invariant proves correctness.

Can an invalid or repeated event mutate valid state?
Are asynchronous or external results stale, missing, or out of order?
Does the representation match the operation mix and constraints?
Did the repair pass the original failure and nearby regression cases?

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Testing strategy and adversarial cases is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Cover empty, minimal, maximal, duplicate, ordered, disconnected, overflow, and constraint-boundary cases relevant to the contract.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Testing strategy and adversarial cases, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

project.title: Mixed Problems, Interview Strategy and Communication: Interview-Ready Algorithm Solution Set
project.real_world_context: A small team needs a timed but explainable problem-solving scenario that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate interview-ready algorithm solution set that demonstrates all eight skills from Mixed Problems, Interview Strategy and Communication. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: Restate the input-output contract, constraints, examples, edge cases, and allowed assumptions before choosing a method.
Start with a correct baseline, locate the operation causing excessive growth, and replace it using structure or precomputation.
Classify order, locality, repetition, hierarchy, connectivity, and optimization structure before selecting a pattern.
Explain initialization, preservation, termination, and why the invariant implies the required result.
Relate time, space, recursion depth, numeric range, and input distribution to actual limits instead of naming Big-O alone.
Cover empty, minimal, maximal, duplicate, ordered, disconnected, overflow, and constraint-boundary cases relevant to the contract.
Narrate decisions, name invariants, check intermediate states, and respond to feedback without abandoning the proven contract.
Trace the first divergent state, repair the cause, rerun targeted tests, then discuss alternatives and trade-offs.

starter_materials.scaffold_policy: Level 5 supplies only constraints, acceptance criteria, and review checkpoints.

mandatory_features: Demonstrate Clarifying ambiguous problem statements and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate From brute force to bottleneck and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Selecting mixed patterns and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Correctness explanations with invariants and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Complexity under realistic constraints and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Testing strategy and adversarial cases and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Communicating while coding and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Debugging and post-solution refinement and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
constraints: Use only the languages, components, or structural interactions supported by the target application environment.
Do not hide invalid input, unavailable data, or failure behind a successful-looking state.
Keep current valid state recoverable until a candidate transition passes validation.
Do not embed secrets, real credentials, personal data, or private endpoints.
Make all important output and error states accessible and testable.
Record assumptions and unsupported cases explicitly.
The submitted result must be reproducible from the included instructions.

test_cases.expected: one correct output and valid next state

test_cases.condition: second valid input with different data

test_cases.expected: accepted only if contract includes it

test_cases.condition: valid retry after a controlled failure

edge_cases: empty or minimum
maximum documented size
duplicate or retry
out-of-order or stale result
malformed or unauthorized input
debugging_checklist: Freeze a reproducible failing input.
Compare expected and observed traces.
Find the first divergent state.
Check the constraint at that transition.
Repair cause before symptoms.
Rerun the failure and adjacent cases.
Confirm state recovery and accessible feedback.
Record the limitation if the case remains unsupported.
completion_checklist: All eight level skills appear in the artifact or evidence.
The input-output contract is complete.
The structural model matches the implementation or decision flow.
All eight required test categories have evidence.
The rubric self-score totals 100 possible points.
No secret, real credential, or sensitive personal data is included.
Submission instructions reproduce the result.
Reflection names one failure, repair, and justified improvement.
submission_requirements: README with setup or review instructions

rubric.evidence: inputs, outputs, constraints, diagram, and milestones
mandatory behavior matches the project contract
clear responsibilities, transitions, and dependency boundaries
normal, boundary, invalid, repeated, and failure cases
usable states, safe handling, and recovery feedback
setup, decisions, limitations, evidence, and reproducible instructions
first divergence, repair, trade-off, and next iteration

common_failure_conditions: The result handles only one normal case.
State changes before validation.
A level skill is named but not demonstrated.
The diagram disagrees with the implemented flow.
A failed dependency leaves a false success state.
Submission evidence cannot be reproduced.
reflection_questions: Which assumption changed after the first trace?
Where did expected and observed state first diverge?
Which invariant prevented the most serious failure?
What trade-off did you make among clarity, cost, performance, accessibility, safety, or flexibility?
What evidence would you collect before a wider release?
optional_extensions: Add a second representation and compare which relationships become easier to inspect.
Add property-based or generated boundary cases without duplicating existing tests.
Measure one performance, quality, or risk indicator and justify an improvement threshold.
Design a migration or compatibility plan for one changed requirement.
project.acceptable_outcome_example: A submission may use the supplied contract and state templates, implement one complete primary journey, show all required failure states, and provide eight passing test records plus one documented limitation. The exact implementation remains the learner's work.

prompts.prompt: Restate the final input-output contract in one sentence.
Describe the first state where expected and observed behavior diverged.
Explain the repair and the invariant or constraint it restored.
Name one design trade-off and the evidence behind your choice.
What is the safest and most valuable next improvement?

optional_mastery_challenge.title: Optional Mastery Transfer
optional_mastery_challenge.prompt: Transfer the level's eight governing rules to a new version of a timed but explainable problem-solving scenario with one changed constraint, one new failure state, and one stricter evidence requirement.
required_outputs: change-impact table across all eight skills
normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery traces
success_criteria: The changed constraint is applied consistently.
No unaffected invariant is silently removed.
The new failure state has visible recovery behavior.
Evidence distinguishes old and new behavior.
